title: One Ant Can Wake a Whole Colony
summary:
Acorn ants rest, as if the nest is asleep. Then they burst into action, like falling dominoes. For more than 30 years, scientists have wondered: with no leader giving orders, what wakes the colony at the same time?

Biologist Simon Garnier of the New Jersey Institute of Technology, with engineers Michael Napoli and Maurizio Porfiri of New York University, tried to find out with math. They shared their findings on August 5 in the journal PRX Life.

Their computer model of a quiet colony showed that one ant is all it takes: when it starts moving, it wakes the ants it meets, who wake others in turn.

But three things must line up. First, activity must travel fast: ants move quickly, or the nest is crowded. Second, ants must wake easily when bumped. Third, the colony must rest before the next spark. Too slow, and it never fully rests; too fast, and the spark dies out. When all three line up, the colony bursts into action. Scientists call this sudden flip a phase transition, like water freezing into ice.
why_it_matters: Watching how ants wake each other up can help you notice how small actions spread through a group, like when one classmate starting a game gets everyone playing.

background_read: Ants live together in big groups called colonies, and they work together even though no single ant is the boss.
Scientists use computer models to test ideas about how groups of animals act, by copying what the animals do in a program.
A phase transition is a sudden change, like water turning into ice, when many small things add up at once.
